methods.label: Use the definition and counterexamples
methods.explanation:
The defining interval lets us prove I for every real \(x\). To disprove either of the other statements, which claim an identity for all inputs, one counterexample is enough.

For I, let \(n=[x]\). By definition,
\[
n\le x<n+1.
\]
Adding \(1\) throughout gives
\[
n+1\le x+1<n+2.
\]
Since \(n+1\) is an integer, this says \([x+1]=n+1=[x]+1\). This argument includes negative numbers and integer inputs, so I is true for all real \(x\).

For II, take \(x=y=\tfrac34\). Then
\[
[x+y]=\left[\tfrac32\right]=1,
\qquad [x]+[y]=0+0=0.
\]
Thus II is false.

For III, take \(x=y=\tfrac32\). Then
\[
[xy]=\left[\tfrac94\right]=2,
\qquad [x][y]=1\cdot1=1.
\]
Thus III is false. Only I is true, choice B.
